title: Why Put Telescopes in Space?
objective: After this level you can explain what Earth’s atmosphere does to starlight and what Hubble gained by leaving it.
summary: Air makes stars twinkle and blocks much of the spectrum. Above it, Hubble (1990) takes sharp images across more wavelengths.

cards.headline: Twinkling is beautiful. For astronomers, it’s a problem.
cards.body: That gentle shimmer isn't the star. It's Earth's air getting in the way. Lovely for lullabies, terrible for photos.

cards.headline: The trouble with air
cards.body: Stars twinkle because moving pockets of air in Earth's atmosphere bend their light back and forth. It's like looking at a coin at the bottom of a swimming pool while the water ripples. Telescopes get that blur too. Worse, the atmosphere blocks most ultraviolet light and X-rays, and much infrared, before they ever reach the ground. Some of the sky's light simply never arrives.

cards.headline: Hubble, above it all
cards.body: The fix: get above the air. The Hubble Space Telescope launched in 1990 and orbits above the atmosphere, so its images are free of that blurring. Up there, the light the atmosphere blocks is no longer out of reach either. And Hubble is the only space telescope designed to be repaired and upgraded by astronauts in orbit. Now that's a house call.

cards.fact: Hubble helped measure the age of the universe.
cards.context: Its observations helped pin the universe's age at about 13.8 billion years, a number you met back in Level 10. Not bad for a telescope whose big advantage is simply being above the weather.

cards.headline: Space telescopes: explained
learned: The atmosphere blocks most UV and X-rays

options.label: They flicker as they burn their fuel
options.rationale: The star’s light is steady; the flicker happens here.

options.label: Moving air in Earth’s atmosphere bends their light
The Moon’s light interferes with them
options.rationale: Twinkling happens with or without the Moon.

options.label: They are spinning very fast
options.rationale: Spinning doesn’t make a star twinkle.

questions.explanation: Turbulent air bends starlight back and forth, making stars appear to twinkle.

questions.prompt: Besides sharper images, what else do telescopes gain by going to space?

options.label: A closer view of the stars
options.rationale: A few hundred km closer makes no difference.

options.label: Protection from meteors
options.rationale: Space actually has more debris risk.

options.label: Access to light the atmosphere blocks, like ultraviolet and X-rays
Freedom from the Sun’s gravity
options.rationale: They’re still in orbit around Earth.

questions.explanation: The atmosphere absorbs most ultraviolet and X-ray light and much infrared. From space, telescopes can see those wavelengths.

questions.prompt: From Level 31: which kinds of light are mostly blocked before they reach the ground?

options.label: Visible light and radio waves
options.rationale: Both reach the ground, which is why we see and use radio.

options.label: Only light from distant galaxies
options.rationale: Blocking depends on wavelength, not distance.

questions.explanation: Earth’s atmosphere absorbs most ultraviolet and X-ray light, which is why those telescopes must go to space.
